project.title: The Meme Ontology
project.description: An OWL 2 knowledge graph of 5,000 internet memes, grounded in bibliographic and iconological theory, with interactive visualizations, a SPARQL explorer and the full thesis online.
project.introText: MEMO is an ontology of internet memes, from my master's research Towards an Ontology of Memes (supervisor Fabio Vitali), which I began as a visiting research fellow at the Institute of Network Cultures in Amsterdam, for its Viral Image Cultures project.

project.middleText: Following Lev Manovich's cultural analytics, it treats memes as a large dataset rather than isolated texts. Around 5,000 images and their metadata, scraped from Know Your Meme, are described in an OWL ontology informed by FRBR across three areas: visual content, cultural references and format. CLIP is used to classify them semi-automatically.
project.conclusionText: The ontology is published with LODE documentation, interactive visualizations of formats, platforms, periods and variants, and a SPARQL explorer with example queries, including links to Wikidata for regions and platforms.

summary.brief: A large, messy cultural dataset with no structured model to classify, link or query it.

summary.method: About 5,000 Know Your Meme entries scraped; an OWL ontology informed by FRBR; CLIP for semi-automatic classification.
summary.outcome: A published ontology (206,923 triples) with documentation, eleven interactive visualizations, a SPARQL explorer linked to Wikidata and the full thesis as an indexed reader.

context.text: Internet memes are one of the largest and least formally organized bodies of visual culture of the twenty-first century. Know Your Meme documents them in depth, but as a community wiki: there was no formal, theory-grounded model to classify meme templates, their visual properties and the way their variants transform them. MEMO (the MEMe Ontology) is that model, built and tested on a corpus of 5,000 entries.

goals.title: A formal model
goals.text: Extend bibliographic (FRBR/LRM) and iconological (Panofsky) frameworks so memes can be classified without flattening their cultural complexity.

goals.title: Culture at corpus scale
goals.text: Make structural patterns in meme culture (formats, platforms, periods, variants) visible and queryable, following Manovich’s cultural analytics.

items.title: Ontological
items.text: Which formal framework can classify memes as cultural and digital objects, and how must FRBR and Panofsky’s iconological method be extended to fit them?

items.title: Computational
items.text: How far can CLIP zero-shot classification describe the pre-iconographical level of 5,000 meme images, and where does it fail?

items.title: Cultural analytics
items.text: Which temporal, relational and platform patterns become visible only when memes are analysed as a corpus?

items.title: Archival
items.text: How can a community archive like Know Your Meme become a machine-readable research corpus while keeping the integrity of its folksonomy metadata?

sections.title: Pipeline
sections.lead: Four stages, each producing the structured input for the next, adapted from Manovich’s operations for cultural analytics.

items.title: Three datasets
items.text: A random sample of 5,000 Know Your Meme entries with images and metadata; D0, a purposive subset of 50; and 391 variant images from the galleries of 43 D0 entries.

items.title: Two axes of classification
items.text: An OWL 2 DL ontology built in Protégé along FRBR/LRM levels (MemeIdea, MemeConcept, VariantInstance) and Panofsky’s levels of meaning, reusing Wikidata, schema.org and Dublin Core.

items.title: CLIP and manual annotation
items.text: CLIP ViT-B/32 zero-shot labels for image type, subject, text and colour on all 5,000 images; hand annotation of cultural references and of how 50 variants transform their template.

items.title: A public web platform
items.text: D3.js visualizations of the whole corpus, D0 and the variants, alongside the ontology documentation, an in-browser SPARQL endpoint and the thesis text.

sections.title: The ontology
sections.lead: 33 classes, 28 object properties and 14 data properties. The main contribution is a transformation typology at the Expression level (TransformationDimension and TransformationExtent), which neither FRBR nor iconography provides: it records how, and how far, a variant departs from its template.

sections.title: Variants and transformation
sections.lead: The D0 sample and its variants show what the ontology’s Expression level adds: a meme’s views and its creative productivity are separate things. Karen has over 13,000 documented variants at 2 million views; Me Gusta has hundreds at 9 million.

items.alt: Scatter plot of the 50 D0 memes by views and number of variants
items.caption: Creative productivity × cultural prominence for the 50 D0 memes, drawn as their images.

items.alt: Rows of variant thumbnails sorted from minimal to parody
items.caption: Variant gallery: 50 annotated variants of five templates, from minimal change to parody.

items.alt: Radial tree with the original meme at the centre and its variants on rings by transformation extent
items.caption: Variant family tree: rings are transformation extent, sectors the main dimension; hovering a variant swaps it into the centre.

sections.title: Exploring the graph
sections.lead: Three views make the knowledge graph and the classifier tangible, rather than only summarising them.

items.alt: Force graph of memes and property chips expanding from one meme
items.caption: Knowledge-graph walk: a meme opens into its properties and a property pulls in other memes that share it; each node links to a SPARQL query.

items.alt: Every meme drawn as a coloured dot on a colour wheel
items.caption: Colour spectrum: all 5,000 memes as their average colour, rearranged by year, hue or lightness.

items.alt: Dot plot of CLIP confidence per image type with a threshold line
items.caption: Classifier confidence: at a 0.80 threshold, 61.7% of CLIP labels would not survive.

sections.title: The thesis, online
sections.lead: The dissertation is published on the site as an indexed reader, generated from the final PDF: 61 headings, full-text search with section context, figures, a linked bibliography and page numbers that match the printed edition.

sections.title: Visual identity
sections.lead: The site had to read as a thesis and as a meme archive at once. Titles use Impact, the typeface of the meme caption; the rest is quiet ink on paper, so the memes are the only colour. Memes from the corpus are used as graphic material: in title strips, on the home wall and in a random-meme card available on every page.

items.title: FRBR, extended, fits memes
items.text: Idea, template and variant are distinct entities that carry different information, and the transformation typology adds what neither FRBR nor iconography models.

items.title: CLIP helps, but cannot be trusted alone
items.text: Image-type labels are plausible (Cartoon 45.3%, Photograph 44.8%), but zero-shot classification always picks a label; 34.4% of subjects fell back to Unknown and the rest lack ground truth.

items.title: Patterns only visible at scale
items.text: Durable foundational formats, the move from static images to short-form video, and format as a predictor of reach.

items.title: Folksonomy as evidence
items.text: Using Wikidata’s publisher property for platform keeps community attributions as assertions rather than claims of objective provenance.

reflection: The ontology works best where it is most theoretical: separating the template from its variants is what made the decoupling of views and variants visible at all.

The weakest layer is the automatic one. Next time I would run several classification passes with different prompts and keep only the labels they agree on, flagging the rest for review: fewer assertions, but ones the analysis can rely on.
Publishing the thesis, the data and the queries together turned a written argument into something people can check and explore themselves.

decisions.choice: Separate the meme template from its variants, following FRBR.
decisions.why: Treating every image as the same kind of thing flattens how variants transform their template.
decisions.result: It made the decoupling of views and variants visible, and led to a transformation typology that neither FRBR nor iconography provides.

decisions.choice: Label all 5,000 images with CLIP, and annotate only 50 variants by hand.
decisions.why: Hand annotation cannot scale to the corpus; zero-shot labels can.
decisions.result: The automatic layer proved the weakest: next time I would keep only the labels several prompts agree on, and flag the rest for review.
